title: Explainable Machine Learning Algorithms for State-of-Health Estimation and Remaining Useful Life Prediction of Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: State-of-health (SOH) estimation and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction address related but distinct aspects of lithium-ion battery degradation. This study evaluates separate XGBoost regressors for SOH estimation and RUL prediction using four NASA Ames lithium-ion cells with complete capacity-fade trajectories. The reference capacity is defined as the median capacity of the first five discharges, while end of life (EOL) is defined as the first subsequent cycle at which capacity falls to or below 80% of this reference. At a fixed observation point of 600~s, the prediction features comprise electrical, thermal, cycle-related, initial-reference, and preceding electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements. Full-discharge capacity and future EOL information are used only to construct retrospective target labels and are excluded from the corresponding predictors. A leave-one-cell-out evaluation yields 351 evaluated cycles. XGBoost achieves pooled SOH and RUL mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 1.157 percentage points and 17.948 cycles, respectively, while ridge regression achieves 1.195 percentage points and 17.611 cycles. The held-out B0006 cell exhibits a substantially higher XGBoost RUL MAE of 34.886 cycles, highlighting the limitations of cross-cell prognostic transfer despite low pooled SOH error. TreeSHAP analysis identifies the change in 600-s voltage relative to the cell's initial reference as the largest average contribution to SOH predictions. Removing this feature increases SOH root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 1.473 to 2.929 percentage points, while reducing RUL RMSE from 22.731 to 20.836 cycles. These findings demonstrate that feature importance and predictive utility differ between SOH estimation and RUL prediction.

title: Measurement Protocol Dependence in Early-Life Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Estimation: A Controlled Study Using NASA PCoE Cells
abstract: Battery management systems must estimate state of health (SOH) early in a cell’s life. This study examines how much of the reported estimation accuracy depends on the measurement protocol rather than the estimator. A physics-based fade curve, Random Forest, XGBoost version 3.3.0, a physics-assisted hybrid and a gated recurrent unit are compared using leave-one-cell-out validation on four NASA PCoE cells over early-life windows of 20–100 cycles. Training and evaluation observations are both drawn from cycles 1 to W; therefore, the primary task is cross-cell SOH estimation within an observed window, not future-cycle forecasting. A separate temporal evaluation yields higher forecasting RMSE, by factors of 1.9–4.3 relative to in-window estimation. At 50 cycles, XGBoost achieves a pooled RMSE of 0.024 SOH units, compared with 0.044 for the fade curve. Removing the recorded discharge duration feature increases RMSE by 34%. In a separate diagnostic comparison, a single time-under-load feature achieves lower RMSE than the full nine-feature set. Neither the fade curve estimate nor cycle index improves XGBoost when added as a feature. On common SOH support, the increase in R2 with window length is attributable to the widening test target distribution. A comparative analysis of four variable-current cells provides complementary evidence.
title_zh: Measurement Protocol Dependence in Early-Life Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Estimation: A Controlled Study Using NASA PCoE Cells

title: Research on State of Health Prediction of Power Batteries for New Energy Vehicles
abstract: The state of health (SOH) of power batteries is a core parameter that characterizes driving-range attenuation, power decline and safety risks of new-energy vehicles.Accurate SOH prediction is of great significance for vehicle energy management, warranty judgment and echelon utilization of retired batteries.This paper defines an SOH characterization system dominated by capacity retention rate and internal resistance growth rate, and analyzes aging mechanisms including solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) film thickening, active-lithium loss and lithium plating, as well as the coupled influences of temperature, state-of-charge window and charge-discharge rate on degradation rates.Existing prediction methods are categorized into model-based, data-driven and mechanismdata fusion approaches, and their accuracy, computing-power requirements and engineering implementability are compared.Furthermore, a vehicle-level prediction framework of "on-board feature extraction -cloud-side model training -cloud-edge collaborative updating" is proposed.Key challenges such as working-condition generalization, label acquisition, battery inconsistency and computing-power constraints are discussed.The analysis reveals that the engineering bottleneck for SOH prediction has shifted from algorithm accuracy to data closed-loop performance and generalization capability.Constructing mechanism-constrained datadriven models calibrated with a small volume of real-vehicle calibration data is a feasible approach to improving practical performance.
venue: International Journal of Science and Engineering Applications

title: GreenRide: A Real Time Ride Hailing and Smart Campus Mobility System for Solar Powered Electric Tricycles at a Nigerian University, with Fleet Simulation on Real Campus Map and Solar Data
abstract: Many African universities are large enough that moving between hostels, faculties, clinics and gates takes a vehicle, yet intra campus transport is often informal. At the University of Port Harcourt, Nigeria, solar powered electric tricycles now carry students inside the campus, but riders find them by waiting at a single charging spot, flagging one down or calling a driver whose number they happen to know. This paper presents GreenRide, a web based ride hailing system for campus solar tricycles, and evaluates how well such a system can serve the campus. GreenRide gives passengers, drivers and administrators separate browser interfaces, matches requests through Socket.io broadcast, shares the driver's live position on an OpenStreetMap map, and stores users and rides in MongoDB behind JSON Web Token authentication with email verification. Because no live fleet was available, we built a simulation of a working day from 07:00 to 19:00 on the real campus, using 193 named campus places and the road network from OpenStreetMap and hourly 2020 solar output for the campus from PVGIS. We compared the informal system with three dispatch rules (GreenRide as built, nearest tricycle, and nearest tricycle with battery checks) across 5 to 30 tricycles, 300 to 1,200 requests per day, and 10 dry season and 10 rainy season days. The informal system never served more than 69 percent of requests, however many tricycles were added. With enough tricycles, GreenRide with nearest tricycle dispatch served every request: at 300 requests per day and 20 tricycles, mean waiting time fell from 9.8 minutes to 4.4 minutes. The broadcast rule now used by GreenRide sent tricycles on long empty trips, about half of all kilometres, and more than doubled waiting time compared with nearest dispatch. When demand exceeded what the fleet could carry, battery energy, not matching, limited the service to about 21 to 24 trips per tricycle per day, and rainy season sunshine, 32 percent lower than dry season sunshine, cut the share served by up to 15 points. We give a fleet sizing rule, a dispatch change and an energy aware charging policy for campus solar tricycle services.

title: AI-Driven Cross-Scale Simulation of Lithium Batteries
abstract: The evolution of lithium battery performance involves complex coupled processes across multiple scales, ranging from electronic and atomic scales to mesoscopic structures and battery systems. Traditional simulation approaches face significant challenges in accurately predicting realistic battery electrochemical responses because of scale-bridging limitations, high computational costs, and insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms. In recent years, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have provided opportunities for cross-scale simulations by enabling knowledge transfer and intelligent prediction through learning physical representations from data. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The review first discusses AI-enabled simulation approaches spanning the micro- to mesoscale, including machine learning potentials (MLPs), AI-driven kinetic Monte Carlo (AI-kMC), AI-driven phase-field modeling (AI-PFM), and AI-driven coarse-grained molecular dynamics (AI-CGMD). It then summarizes meso- to macroscale methodologies, including surrogate models, reduced-order modeling, and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Furthermore, AI applications in multiscale feature fusion, inverse materials design, and battery design automation (BDA) are discussed together with computational paradigms toward digital twins and intelligent battery research and development. Despite substantial advances, several critical challenges, including limited model generalization and insufficient uncertainty quantification, remain. Integrating foundation models, generative AI, and multiscale physical modeling could enable more accurate and computationally efficient battery simulation frameworks. These advances may accelerate the discovery, optimization, and deployment of next-generation energy-storage technologies.
